title: Variables and Data Types
description: Java's eight primitive types, reference types, literals, constants, and local variable type inference.
objectives: Know all eight primitive types and their general size/range
Distinguish primitive types from reference types
Use var for local variable type inference where appropriate

content.heading: Primitive Types
content.body: Java has exactly eight primitive types, each with a fixed size, unlike Python where int has arbitrary precision: byte (8-bit integer), short (16-bit), int (32-bit, the default integer type), long (64-bit, literals suffixed with L, e.g. 10000000000L), float (32-bit floating point, literals suffixed with f), double (64-bit floating point, the default for decimal literals), char (a single 16-bit Unicode character, in single quotes: 'A'), and boolean (true or false only — unlike C, Java does not treat integers as booleans). Every variable must be declared with an explicit type before use: int age = 21;.

content.heading: Reference Types, Literals, Constants, and var
content.body:
Anything that isn't one of the eight primitives is a reference type: String, arrays, and every class (including wrapper classes like Integer). A reference type variable holds a reference to an object on the heap, not the object's data directly (this parallels Python's model of names referencing objects, but Java's primitives are genuinely different — they hold their value directly, with no object involved).

final marks a variable as a constant: once assigned, it cannot be reassigned (final int MAX_SIZE = 100;). Since Java 10, the var keyword lets the compiler infer a local variable's type from its initializer (var name = "Asha"; infers String) — this is type inference, not dynamic typing: the type is still fixed at compile time, var is just a shorthand for the compiler to figure out and enforce that type, and it can only be used for local variables with an initializer, never for fields or method parameters.

content.explanation: Each primitive is explicitly typed. var infers String from the string literal at compile time — name is still statically typed as String, it's just not spelled out.

keyPoints: Java has exactly 8 primitive types: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean
Everything else (String, arrays, classes) is a reference type, holding a reference to a heap object
final makes a variable a constant — assignable only once
var infers a local variable's type at compile time; it does not make Java dynamically typed
commonMistakes: Confusing var (compile-time type inference) with Python-style dynamic typing
Forgetting the L or f suffix on long/float literals when needed
Trying to use a boolean where an int (or vice versa) is expected — Java does not auto-convert between them
